chapters.title: Chapter 1: Two Different Businesses Under One Name

lessons.title: Residential vs Commercial: What Actually Separates Them

children.text: Two investors in Bengaluru each put ₹1.2 crore into property in the same month. One buys a 2BHK in Whitefield and rents it to a young IT couple for ₹30,000 a month. The other buys a 1,000 sq ft office unit a few kilometres away, already leased to a mid-sized software firm at ₹75,000 a month. Same city, same cheque, and they have bought two completely different businesses. This lesson maps the six differences that separate residential from commercial property, so everything later in this course has a frame to hang on.

body.text: A home is priced by what the neighbours paid. A commercial property is priced by the rent it produces. Almost every other difference between the two flows from that one fact.

children.text: The Two Categories, Defined

Residential property is built for people to live in: apartments, independent houses, villas and residential plots. Commercial property is built for businesses to earn money in: offices, shops, mall units, warehouses and industrial sheds. The land-use classification and the building's approvals decide which one a property legally is, not what the current occupant does with it. A flat used as a dental clinic is still, on paper, a residential flat, and that matters for loans, property tax and whether the housing society can object.
Difference 1: Who Pays the Rent

Residential tenants are households. They pay from salary, move when they change jobs, and rarely sign for more than a year. Commercial tenants are businesses. They pay from revenue, spend lakhs on fit-outs they do not want to abandon, and sign leases running three to nine years. In one case you are underwriting a family's stability; in the other, a company's balance sheet. The next lesson goes deep on this.
Difference 2: How the Price Is Set

Ask a Whitefield broker what a 2BHK is worth and you will hear what similar flats in the same society sold for recently. That is comparable-sales pricing, and it is shaped heavily by sentiment, school proximity and how badly one buyer wants that particular home. Rent barely enters the conversation.

markDefs.definition: Net Operating Income divided by property value. It is the yield buyers are willing to accept for a commercial asset; a lower cap rate means a higher price for the same income.

children.text: Commercial property is valued the way an analyst values a bond or a dividend stock: by the income it produces. The key tool is the
capitalisation rate, or cap rate

body.caption: Net Operating Income is annual rent minus the owner's operating costs, such as property tax and any landlord-borne maintenance.

children.text: For simplicity, assume the tenant bears maintenance and ignore property tax, so the office unit's ₹9 lakh a year of rent is its net operating income. If buyers in that micro-market accept a 7.5% cap rate, the unit is worth ₹9 lakh ÷ 0.075 = ₹1.2 crore. Raise the rent and the value rises mechanically. Lose the tenant and the value falls, because a vacant unit has no income to capitalise.

body.text: This is why listed REITs on NSE and BSE, such as Embassy Office Parks REIT and Nexus Select Trust, put occupancy and weighted average lease expiry at the front of every investor presentation. For a commercial asset, the lease is the value.

body.title: Show me the math: what a 15% rent escalation does to value

children.text: The office unit earns ₹9 lakh a year. Its lease has a 15% escalation after three years, taking rent to ₹9 lakh × 1.15 = ₹10.35 lakh. At the same 7.5% cap rate, value becomes ₹10.35 lakh ÷ 0.075 = ₹1.38 crore.

The owner gained ₹18 lakh of value without the market moving at all, purely because the contract said so. A residential flat has no equivalent mechanism: its rent is renegotiated at each renewal and its price moves with the neighbourhood.

children.text: The gap is real and persistent. Residential yields in big Indian cities usually sit around 2% to 3.5%, on homes let through 11-month
leave and licence agreements

offices and warehouses typically trade at 7% to 9% on leases that lock income in for years. But the yield number alone misleads, which is why Difference 6 exists.
Difference 4: Ticket Size and Financing

A decent flat costs ₹50 to ₹80 lakh in cities like Jaipur, Indore or Coimbatore, and a home loan is the cheapest secured credit most Indians will ever get. Commercial property usually needs a bigger cheque, and lenders treat it more like a business loan: higher interest rates, a smaller share of the value financed, and shorter tenures. Chapter 4 compares home loans with lease rental discounting in detail.
Difference 5: Costs and Tax

Rent from both types is taxed under "Income from House Property", with a 30% standard deduction on the net annual value, and profits on sale of either count as long-term capital gains after 24 months of holding. GST is where they split. Renting a home to a family for residential use is exempt from GST. Renting a shop or office is a taxable service. (One exception: if a GST-registered business rents a flat, that business pays GST under reverse charge.)

body.label: GST on commercial rent
body.context: Applies once the landlord's aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh a year (lower in a few special category states). Rent on a home let for residential use is exempt.

children.text: Difference 6: How Risk Shows Up

Residential risk arrives often, in small doses. Tenants leave every year or two, the flat sits empty for a month, you repaint and re-list. When you sell, buyers are plentiful, because almost every household is a potential buyer.

Commercial risk arrives rarely, in large doses. A tenant may stay nine years, but when it leaves, finding the next one can take six months to a year or more. You earn nothing in that time and may still pay maintenance and property tax. The pool of buyers is also narrower: investors, businesses and funds, not every salaried family.

body.text: Run the numbers before you get excited about 7.5%. If the office unit sits empty for 12 months once in five years, you collect four years of rent over five: 7.5% × 4 ÷ 5 = 6.0% average gross yield, before brokerage and the maintenance you pay while it is empty. Still double the flat's 3%, but no longer the gap it first appeared to be.

body.title: Quick Check: Pricing Logic
body.question: A pre-leased office unit's tenant renews at 10% higher rent. The local cap rate is unchanged. What happens to the unit's value?
options: It stays the same, because prices depend on comparable sales
It rises by roughly 10%, because value is income divided by cap rate
It falls, because higher rent increases vacancy risk
It rises only if nearby units also sell for more
body.explanation: Commercial value = Net Operating Income ÷ Cap Rate. Income is up 10% and the cap rate is unchanged, so value rises by about 10%. The first option describes how flats are priced, and the last mixes the two methods.

body.title: Calculate: Gross Yield on a Pune Shop
body.prompt: A shop in Wakad, Pune costs ₹80 lakh and is rented at ₹48,000 a month. What is its gross rental yield?

body.title: Scenario: "Only a Fool Buys Residential"
body.scenario: A colleague in Gurugram has ₹1 crore saved. She says: "Flats yield 3%, offices yield 8%. Only a fool buys residential." She plans to put the entire amount into one small office unit in a new building on Sohna Road that has no tenant yet.
body.prompt: What is wrong with her reasoning?
body.modelAnswer: Four things. First, the 8% figure describes leased, Grade A assets. An unleased unit in a new building yields 0% until someone signs, which can take a year or more. Second, commercial value is income divided by cap rate, so with no tenant the unit's value rests largely on hope. Third, putting all ₹1 crore into one unit with one future tenant is extreme concentration, and the resale buyer pool is much narrower than for a flat. Fourth, she is ignoring GST compliance once rent crosses the threshold, plus maintenance and property tax during vacancy. None of this makes residential the better choice. It means she should compare like with like, for example a pre-leased unit with a proven tenant, or a REIT, and check actual leasing activity in that micro-market before committing.

points: Residential property is priced mainly on comparable sales and sentiment; commercial property is priced on income divided by cap rate.
Big-city residential yields sit around 2% to 3.5%, while leased Grade A offices and warehouses typically offer 7% to 9%.
Homes are let on 11-month agreements; commercial leases run 3 to 9 years with lock-ins and built-in escalations.
Commercial property needs bigger tickets and costlier loans, and its rent attracts 18% GST above the turnover threshold.
Residential risk is frequent and small; commercial risk is rare and large, because one vacancy can erase a year's income.
Always compare like with like: a leased asset against a leased asset, with vacancy and costs included.

body.text: Yields, escalation terms and tax thresholds in this lesson are indicative figures for major Indian cities as of 2026 and vary by micro-market, building quality and individual lease. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy any property.
